title: Chasing the shadow
text: A total solar eclipse lasts minutes, and the {{1}} (LIKELY) of any particular town standing in the Moon's shadow is tiny — roughly once every four hundred years, for London. That scarcity explains the eclipse chasers, a tribe of enthusiasts who will cross continents, charter ships or climb mountains, all for a spectacle witnesses struggle to describe and universally call {{2}} (FORGET). As totality approaches, the light turns silver, the temperature drops, birds are betrayed into silence by the {{3}} (SUDDEN) of the darkness, and stars emerge at midday. Then the corona blazes around the black disc, and sober scientists become whooping {{4}} (ENTHUSIAST). Science has richly rewarded such devotion: helium was identified in the Sun's atmosphere during the eclipse of 1868 and only {{5}} (SUBSEQUENT) found on Earth, while the famous starlight measurements of 1919 made Einstein famous {{6}} (NIGHT). Satellites can now imitate an eclipse artificially, yet researchers still travel to the shadow's path, because the ground-based view of the inner corona remains {{7}} (MATCH). The chasers themselves, meanwhile, admit that their hobby is quietly {{8}} (ADDICT): one totality, they warn, is never enough.

gaps.explanation: 'universally call unforgettable' — negative prefix un- on the adjective.
'the suddenness of the darkness' — noun from sudden.
'scientists become whooping enthusiasts' — plural pinned by the plural subject.
'only subsequently found on Earth' — adverb from subsequent.
'made Einstein famous overnight' — prefix over- + night.
'remains unmatched' — negative prefix un- on the participle.
